title: Restoration of volitional function after complete spinal cord transection

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an operation or operative biological reconstruction that restores useful communication across a chronically and anatomically severed spinal cord. Its goal is voluntary movement, reproducible sensation and meaningful autonomic function below the injury, with recovery sufficient to support daily activities. This remains a breakthrough target: the supplied studies do not demonstrate biological reconstruction across a chronic, anatomically complete transection.

Conceptual synthesis: reconstruction could use regenerated host axons, graft-derived neuronal relays or another biological connection that carries useful signals across the lesion. Growing axons and forming synapses are intermediate achievements; the essential capability is coordinated communication that produces useful function. Exact reconnection of every relevant neuron to its original target is not established as a necessary condition by the supplied evidence.

Anatomical completeness is central to the concept. A clinical classification of AIS A, often described as a complete injury, does not by itself establish that the cord is physically severed. Improvements after clinically complete injuries can therefore be important without demonstrating repair of a complete anatomical gap. The same distinction applies to neuroprosthetic assistance and gains attributed to plasticity in residual pathways.

significance.text: If achieved, durable biological restoration across a chronic complete transection would create a major new surgical capability: recovering useful communication through previously disconnected spinal pathways. The unmet goal is substantial; the July 2026 human cell-therapy report explicitly described restoration of damaged spinal circuitry as a capability no therapy then provided. That dated statement supports the importance of the target, although it does not establish an exhaustive account of the field through November 2026.

Conditional impact synthesis: practical benefits would depend on the injury level, the pathways reconstructed and the condition of the systems below the lesion. Useful hand movement, walking, sensation, bladder function and blood-pressure control would each require their own demonstration. Evidence of axonal growth or improvement in one motor task would not establish all these outcomes. Where appropriate to the injury, independent community walking would represent a greater functional achievement than assisted stepping.

Neuroprostheses and therapies that improve function through remaining pathways can deliver meaningful benefits before complete biological reconstruction becomes possible. The reported restoration of self-feeding using a hybrid cortical interface, stimulation and orthosis illustrates that distinction. Such benefits are valuable in their own right, but do not demonstrate that a completely severed cord has been biologically reconnected.

Successful spinal reconstruction could inform other central-nervous-system regeneration problems, including restoring vision after whole-eye transplantation. Transfer would be conditional: retinal viability alone does not restore vision, and useful visual signaling requires additional functional integration. Long-gap peripheral-nerve reconstruction is another related problem, but its different anatomy prevents spinal success from establishing peripheral-nerve repair, or the reverse.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reliable biological transmission across a chronic complete lesion that supports coordinated voluntary, sensory and autonomic function. Axonal extension and synapse formation are relevant steps, but do not alone establish useful reconstruction. The primate graft study reports extensive axonal growth and host synapses in partial-injury models; those achievements do not resolve the complete-transection problem or establish that the original wiring must be reproduced exactly.

Engineering synthesis: a successful reconstruction would need to bridge the lesion, sustain appropriate cells and connections, integrate signals with downstream circuits, and translate that integration into controllable function. Regenerated host pathways and graft-derived relays are possible approaches. Useful connections must be distinguished from anatomical growth that does not contribute to behavior, and functional gains must be distinguished from assistance or compensation through spared tissue.

The earlier research identifies cavities, glial scarring, inflammation and long regeneration distances as potential obstacles in chronic human injuries. These remain relevant barrier hypotheses, but the supplied review does not adequately substantiate their extent, relative importance or treatment requirements in chronic complete human transection. They should not be treated here as a fully documented mechanistic account. The evidence also leaves unresolved how to achieve durable reconstruction at human scale without unacceptable treatment or graft-related harm.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes a 2023 mouse result to Squair and colleagues: directing a characterized neuronal population toward its natural lumbar target region reportedly produced substantial walking recovery after complete spinal injury, whereas growth across the lesion alone did not. The Science citation is supplied, but its journal page did not open in the initial research pass and no source text was retained for the validated review. The reported walking and target-specificity findings therefore remain unverified within this evidence package. That access limitation does not show that the findings are false.

Sinopoulou and colleagues reported primate neural-stem-cell transplantation results online on November 17, 2025, with assignment to an October 2026 Nature Biotechnology issue. Human embryonic-stem-cell-derived spinal neural stem cells improved skilled hand performance after hemisection or hemicontusion. In grafted hemisected subjects, fine-object retrieval success reached 53.4% ± 19.2%. The abstract also reports grafts extending up to hundreds of thousands of axons into host circuits as far as 39 mm below the injury and forming synapses with host circuitry. These are partial-injury models, not complete transections. The authors also describe sufficient functional recovery through cell therapy as an unmet goal.

The primate findings are supported here by subscription-preview material, principally the abstract. The supplied supplement yielded almost no extractable text, so it did not permit verification of detailed methods or figures. The reported retrieval percentage and anatomical observations can be preserved as reported outcomes, but the available material does not support a full methodological appraisal or extension of the findings to chronic complete human injury.

A first-in-human, open-label phase 1 study by Sugai and colleagues, published online July 21, 2026, treated four people with subacute clinically complete cervical injury using iPSC-derived neural stem/progenitor cells. The abstract reports no tumor formation or graft-related adverse events during 2–4 years of follow-up. Median improvement in the International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury motor score, measured from a baseline two weeks after injury to week 52, was 13 points, with a range of 10–40. Two participants changed from AIS A to C or D.

These human findings are exploratory observations from four participants, rather than established efficacy or general safety. The open-label design and subacute treatment setting limit attribution of recovery to the graft. Clinical completeness does not establish anatomical transection, and the study does not demonstrate reconstruction across a chronic complete gap. The supplied review had an abstract record with figure captions, rather than the full paper.

A July 2026 single-participant neuroprosthesis report described functional gains in a person with AIS A tetraplegia. The system combined a cortical interface, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, an active hand orthosis, and spinal and cortical neuromodulation. It enabled activities including self-feeding, drinking from a cup and manipulation of delicate objects. The report also described persistent motor and sensory gains attributed to plasticity involving residual pathways. It therefore represents both assistance and therapeutic gains, without demonstrating anatomical reconstruction across a proven complete gap.

The neuroprosthesis PDF was only partially inspectable through its extraction: some pages contained little or no extractable text, some form content was skipped, and figures were not visually inspected in the supplied review. The retained text supports the system components, functional examples and residual-pathway interpretation, but should not be treated as a complete inspection of every figure or supplementary result.

The 2024 report of the first combined whole-eye and face transplant documented a viable, perfused transplanted eye and retinal electrical responses through the first year. At postoperative day 366, the recipient had no light perception in that eye. The article also reported suggestive visual-pathway measurements and called for further testing of reconnection or regrowth. Functional optic-nerve reconnection was not established; the findings do not justify a categorical claim that no anatomical reconnection occurred. The supplied review covered the main article, but not supplementary material or figure images.

Evidence boundary: these dated reports document partial advances and relevant comparators, without establishing the proposed innovation. The supplied record contains no bounded freshness search showing whether additional work changed the picture by November 1, 2026. This record therefore describes the supplied evidence rather than claiming an exhaustive current survey.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: first establish reconstruction in a large animal with a chronic, anatomically complete spinal cord transection, then demonstrate useful recovery in people with chronic complete injury whose anatomy is carefully characterized. Clinical AIS A classification alone would not establish a severed cord. The demonstration should show biological communication across the reconstructed lesion and distinguish its contribution from device assistance, spared pathways and spontaneous recovery.
completion_criteria.label: Biological communication across chronic complete transections in large animals and humans

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional bar: recovery should include voluntary movement against gravity, reproducible sensation and clinically meaningful autonomic function below the lesion, sustained for at least one year. Recipients should perform prespecified tasks they could not perform before treatment. Numerical thresholds, baseline measurements, assistance permitted during testing and clinically meaningful changes should be specified in advance. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus or regulatory requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Below-lesion motor, sensory and autonomic recovery sustained for one year

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: evaluate walking, hand use, sensory discrimination and individual autonomic functions separately, according to lesion level and preserved downstream anatomy. Independent community ambulation, where anatomically relevant, would be a higher bar than assisted stepping. Report the rehabilitation burden, dependence on continuing assistance, variability among recipients and durability of benefit, alongside graft-related adverse events and other treatment harms.
completion_criteria.label: Report function-specific outcomes, practical burdens and harms within anatomical limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility bar: convincing evidence should include appropriate comparison groups, independent outcome assessment, repeated measurements and replication beyond a single subject or laboratory. Anatomical, physiological and behavioral findings should converge on reconstruction as the mechanism of recovery. Results should establish the injury types, chronicity and functional domains actually demonstrated. Finite studies can establish that breadth; they cannot prove that the approach works for every complete spinal injury.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated evidence establishes reconstruction-mediated recovery and its demonstrated scope

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison — SUR-05, Adult surgical wounds that heal by regeneration rather than fibrosis: both concepts concern restoring functional tissue rather than ending with a scar. Spinal reconstruction adds the requirement that neural connections carry useful signals across the injury. Regenerative wound healing could contribute to a favorable repair environment without itself establishing restored spinal communication; conversely, successful spinal reconstruction would not establish regenerative healing across adult surgical wounds generally.

Roster comparison — SUR-09, Living, perfused autologous replacements for complex parts that grafts do not supply, and SUR-12, Life-sustaining autologous solid organs assembled for implantation: all involve constructing living replacements and integrating them with a recipient. SUR-04 is distinguished by the need for functional neural communication across a lesion. The cited cell studies use human embryonic-stem-cell-derived or iPSC-derived cells; their descriptions do not establish an autologous reconstruction. Neither complex-part replacement nor assembled solid organs should be merged with spinal repair.

Roster comparison — SUR-01, Operational donor-specific tolerance for the transplants patients actually receive: donor-specific tolerance could be relevant if spinal reconstruction uses donor-derived cells or tissue. It addresses the recipient's immune response to a graft, whereas SUR-04 addresses useful neural reconnection. Success in either capability would not establish the other, and an autologous approach would have a different relationship to donor-specific tolerance.

Roster comparison — SUR-11, Real-time cellular and molecular vision of the intact operative field: better visualization could potentially help characterize a lesion, place a reconstruction or monitor relevant tissue. That is a possible enabling relationship, not evidence that visualization can create functional neural connections. SUR-11 remains a distinct operative sensing capability.

Related approaches outside the roster include neuroprosthetic bypasses, rehabilitation-mediated plasticity, optic-nerve reconnection after whole-eye transplantation and long-gap peripheral-nerve reconstruction. The neuroprosthesis study demonstrates useful function through a hybrid assistive and therapeutic system, while the eye-transplant report separates tissue viability from restored perception. These comparisons clarify why functional outcomes and mechanism both matter; they do not establish interchangeable solutions across these anatomies.

change_log.change: Preserved SUR-04 and its title while defining the target as operative biological reconstruction across a chronic, anatomically complete transection.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent even though individual supporting assertions require qualification.

change_log.change: Replaced the universal original-target requirement with functional communication through regenerated axons, graft-derived relays or other useful biological connections.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not establish exact restoration of original neuronal targets as necessary for every successful reconstruction.

change_log.change: Retained cavities, scarring, inflammation and distance as explicitly qualified barrier hypotheses.
change_log.reason: These details are useful research context, but the supplied review does not adequately substantiate their chronic human application.

change_log.change: Separated anatomical transection from clinical AIS A classification throughout.
change_log.reason: Clinical completeness does not establish physical severance or exclude contributions from residual pathways.

change_log.change: Preserved the reported mouse findings with an explicit evidence-access limitation.
change_log.reason: No retained source text was available to the review; that prevents verification within this package without demonstrating falsity.

change_log.change: Integrated primate publication timing, retrieval performance, axonal counts, extension distance and partial-injury scope.
change_log.reason: These details explain the achievement while preventing extrapolation to complete transection; preview and supplement limitations constrain appraisal.

change_log.change: Replaced a broad human safety claim with observed adverse-event findings and characterized motor gains as exploratory.
change_log.reason: Four open-label participants do not establish general safety, efficacy or repair of a chronic anatomical gap.

change_log.change: Expanded the neuroprosthesis account to include neuromuscular stimulation, the active orthosis and persistent plasticity-associated gains.
change_log.reason: The earlier bypass description omitted components essential to interpreting the functional results and understated the reported therapeutic gains.

change_log.change: Qualified the eye-transplant conclusion as absence of established functional reconnection.
change_log.reason: No light perception was reported, but suggestive pathway measurements prevent a categorical anatomical conclusion.

change_log.change: Made specific motor and autonomic benefits conditional and expanded proposed demonstrations to address mechanism, replication and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: Individual functional outcomes require separate evidence; the one-year duration and other thresholds are proposals rather than established standards.

change_log.change: Added distinct roster relationships and an explicit freshness boundary.
change_log.reason: Related innovations should remain separate, and the supplied dated reports do not establish an exhaustive November 2026 state of the field.

unresolved_issues: The mouse walking-recovery and target-specificity findings cannot be verified from retained source text in the supplied package.
The chronic human roles of cavities, scarring, inflammation and regeneration distance remain insufficiently documented here.
The primate preview and nearly unextractable supplement do not permit full appraisal of methods, variability or the anatomical basis of recovery.
The four-person human trial leaves efficacy, general safety, mechanism and applicability to chronic anatomically complete injury unresolved.
The neuroprosthesis report does not establish the relative contribution of each system component to every gain; extraction limitations also restrict complete appraisal.
The eye-transplant findings leave the extent of anatomical reconnection or regrowth unresolved despite the absence of demonstrated light perception.
Human verification of anatomical completeness and convincing attribution of recovery to reconstructed pathways require further methodological specification.
Appropriate functional thresholds, acceptable risks, rehabilitation burden and durability beyond the proposed one-year minimum remain to be defined.
No supplied freshness search establishes whether later findings changed these conclusions by November 1, 2026.

brief.title: Restoring movement and feeling after a severed spinal cord
possible: People whose spinal cord has long been completely severed could regain movement they control, reliable feeling and control of functions such as their bladder. Surgery would restore living connections across the break, allowing recovery that supports daily activities.
why: Regaining hand use, walking or bladder control would change how people with paralysis manage everyday life. Repairing disconnected spinal pathways would give surgeons a way to restore functions lost through the injury.

sources.showed: This mouse study examined walking recovery after directing regrowing nerve fibres toward their natural target region following complete spinal injury.
sources.cited_for: It supports the importance of where new nerve connections lead.
sources.not_established: It does not establish repair of a longstanding, completely severed spinal cord in people.

sources.showed: Transplanted cells capable of developing into spinal nerve cells improved skilled hand use in primates with partial spinal injuries. The grafts grew nerve fibres and formed connections with existing nerve cells.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates hand recovery and new nerve connections after cell transplantation in primates.
sources.not_established: The injuries left part of the spinal cord intact, so the results do not establish repair across a complete break.

sources.showed: Four people received cells capable of developing into nerve cells soon after neck-level spinal injuries. Movement scores improved, and no tumours or graft-related harms were observed during follow-up.
sources.quote: with no tumor formation or graft-related adverse events observed
sources.cited_for: It provides early human observations of cell transplantation after spinal injury.
sources.not_established: The small study lacked a blinded comparison and did not establish treatment effectiveness or repair across a longstanding complete break.

sources.who: The double neural bypass study team
sources.showed: A brain interface combined with electrical stimulation and a powered hand support enabled a participant with paralysis to feed himself and handle delicate objects. Some movement and feeling gains persisted.
sources.quote:
this hybrid approach enabled recovery of functional abilities including 
self-feeding and manipulation of delicate objects
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates useful daily activities through a system that assists movement and promotes recovery.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate biological repair across a proven complete break, or establish each component's contribution to recovery.

sources.showed: A transplanted eye survived with blood flow and electrical responses to light, but the recipient could not perceive light.
sources.quote: Serial electroretinography confirmed retinal responses to light in the transplanted eye.
sources.cited_for: It illustrates why living tissue and electrical responses alone do not establish restored perception.
sources.not_established: Useful reconnection between the eye and brain was not established.

shown: Sinopoulou and colleagues improved skilled hand use in primates using transplanted nerve-forming cells, but the injuries were partial. Sugai and colleagues observed movement gains in four people treated soon after injury; their study could not establish how much recovery the graft caused.
missing: Living connections have yet to carry useful signals reliably across a longstanding, completely severed spinal cord in people.
Coordinated movement, feeling and automatic body functions have yet to recover together through such a repair.
Durable recovery at human scale has yet to be demonstrated with acceptable treatment harms and rehabilitation demands.

milestones.label: Living connections carry signals across a longstanding complete break
milestones.explanation: Repair would first have to carry signals across a longstanding complete break in large animals, then support useful recovery in people with carefully established anatomy. This would distinguish repair from devices or surviving pathways.

milestones.label: Movement, feeling and automatic functions recover for a year
milestones.explanation: Recovery would have to include movement against gravity, reliable feeling and meaningful automatic functions such as bladder control for a year, using tasks and thresholds set beforehand. This would establish lasting, useful recovery.

milestones.label: Daily abilities, treatment burdens and harms are established
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to assess each relevant ability separately and report rehabilitation, assistance, harms and variation in lasting benefit. This would establish what recipients can actually do within the limits of their injury.

milestones.label: Independent studies confirm recovery through reconstructed connections
milestones.explanation: Repeated studies would need comparison groups, independent assessments and converging evidence that repaired connections cause recovery. This would establish which injuries and functions benefit beyond a single person or laboratory.

uncertain: How can researchers establish that a human spinal cord is completely severed and that new connections cause recovery?
What levels of recovery, treatment risk and rehabilitation burden should count as success?
How long would useful recovery last beyond the proposed minimum of a year?

page.title: Voluntary motor recovery after chronic paralysis from complete spinal cord transection
page.definition: After at least 12 months of paralysis, a person regains intentional movement below a complete spinal cord transection because biological connections carry commands from the brain across the original gap. Complete transection means the cord was severed across its entire width. Grade A on the American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale records the absence of sensory and motor function in the lowest sacral segments. In a 2014 case, a man graded AIS A regained some voluntary leg movement after grafting and rehabilitation, but a 2-mm rim of tissue had connected the cord ends before surgery.

goal.need: In 2021, about 15.4 million people lived with spinal cord injury worldwide. The number with chronic anatomical transection is unknown. Rehabilitation and assistive equipment help people manage daily activities. When the cord is fully severed, no surviving nerve fibres cross the gap to carry commands from the brain. Depending on the injury level and the movement recovered, a person could eat, dress or walk with less help. Bowel and bladder control are separate goals.

statements.body: Institute of Medicine, Committee on Spinal Cord Injury
statements.quote: the ultimate goal of fully restoring to the individual the levels of activity and function that he or she had before injury.
statements.context: The committee's definition of a cure encompasses sensory, motor, bowel, bladder, autonomic and sexual functions.

statements.body: Wrocław Walk Again programme, sponsored by the Nicholls Spinal Injury Foundation
statements.quote: functional regeneration of severed spinal cord axons
statements.context: The registered study NCT03933072 planned biological reconstruction in two people with anatomically complete transection and included walking independence among its outcomes.

completion.title: Biological reconstruction restores voluntary movement in a confirmatory trial of chronic cord transection.
completion.criterion: A multicentre, controlled Phase 3 trial shows a statistically significant benefit on a prespecified measure of voluntary movement below the lesion, with an acceptable adverse-event profile. Before repair, participants had documented discontinuity across the whole cord and at least 12 months of paralysis. Anatomical and physiological evidence attributes recovered transmission to the repair. The protocol justifies the between-group difference it is powered to detect by its clinical importance and specifies the statistical test and follow-up. Sensory recovery, a change in AIS grade or an evoked response alone cannot establish voluntary movement.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; indication-specific proposal based on published SCI definitions and trial conventions.
completion.threshold_quote: the minimal effect that has clinical relevance in the management of patients.
completion.basis: The ICCP panel defines the general Phase 3 trial convention and the basis for choosing a target effect size. The Atlas applies it to voluntary movement transmitted across a biologically repaired transection. The 12-month boundary comes from the clinical guideline's definition of chronic SCI. No external body identified a universal motor-score increment, follow-up interval or completion test for this exact indication.

milestones.title: Previously severed axons grow beyond an anatomically complete spinal cord lesion in an adult mammal.
milestones.criterion: In an adult mammal, tracing shows that previously severed axons extend beyond the lesion into spinal cord tissue on the far side. Systematic histological sampling across the full width of the cord documents lesion completeness and distinguishes regrowth from fibres spared by the injury.
milestones.set_by: Tuszynski and Steward, 2012, Summary of Guidelines for Demonstrating Axonal Regeneration; published methodological convention.
milestones.threshold_quote: Use of a model in which regenerated axons can be definitively distinguished from spared axons.

milestones.title: Regenerated connections make a causal contribution to movement after complete spinal cord injury.
milestones.criterion: After an anatomically complete lesion in an adult mammal, an experiment links recovery of a measured movement to regenerated connections across the lesion. Selective inactivation is one such test: silencing the neurons whose axons regenerated impairs the recovered movement, while the same manipulation in an appropriate control group leaves movement intact.
milestones.set_by: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, RFA-NS-04-004, on establishing mechanisms of functional recovery. Squair and colleagues supply the selective-inactivation test.
milestones.threshold_quote:
elucidate the mechanisms that underlie recovery induced by
    neuroprotection or repair strategies in animal models

milestones.title: A biological repair reaches first human use in chronic, anatomically complete spinal cord transection.
milestones.criterion: After preclinical safety evaluation, a Phase 1 study administers the biological repair to its first participant with documented anatomical discontinuity across the whole spinal cord and paralysis lasting at least 12 months before treatment.
milestones.set_by: ICCP Clinical Guidelines Panel, clinical trial design, Phase 1; general SCI first-use convention, restricted here to the entry's indication.
milestones.threshold_quote: the first administration of the therapeutic intervention

milestones.title: A controlled Phase 2 study shows a motor benefit after repair of chronic anatomical cord transection.
milestones.criterion: A controlled Phase 2 study finds a benefit of biological repair on a measure of voluntary movement below the lesion. Participants had documented discontinuity across the whole cord and at least 12 months of paralysis before treatment. The person measuring the outcome or evaluating the outcome data is blinded to treatment assignment.
milestones.set_by: ICCP Clinical Guidelines Panel, clinical trial design, Phase 2; general SCI exploratory-efficacy convention.
milestones.threshold_quote: a positive change in relevant outcome variables

milestones.title: Biological repair begun after complete cord injury becomes chronic improves motor function in rodents.
milestones.criterion: Begin repair after an anatomically complete injury has become chronic in the rodent model. Compare motor function with matched injured controls and demonstrate a statistically significant benefit. The recommended treatment delay is at least three months unless the targeted biological process has a different time course. Six weeks is a feasible but less preferred delay.
milestones.set_by: Anderson and colleagues, Recommended guidelines for studies of human subjects with spinal cord injury, preclinical recommendations for chronic regenerative therapies.
milestones.threshold_quote: 3-month or longer time periods constitute optimal rodent data for a chronic study.

not_found: No published consensus or regulatory completion threshold specific to biological repair of chronic anatomical spinal cord transection was found.
No controlled human efficacy result establishing reconstruction-mediated voluntary recovery after chronic anatomical transection was found.
No population estimate specific to chronic anatomical spinal cord transection was found.
No academy or spinal cord society position was found that rejects pursuing voluntary motor recovery after chronic anatomical transection.

results.finding: After T8 crush, traced corticospinal axons extended up to 3 mm beyond the lesion in adult mice with delayed Pten deletion (6 treated, 5 controls).
results.detail: No labeled corticospinal axons were found 5 mm distal to the lesion, and the distal main corticospinal bundle lacked PKCγ staining.
results.quote: Numerous axons also regrew into the injury site and across the lesion for up to 3 mm

results.finding: Adult mice had over 100-fold more traced axon regrowth past the lesion centre than injured controls. Group sizes are given as plot dots.
results.detail: Distal tracer checks found essentially no labelled axons at 3 mm in mice or 5 mm in rats. These checks support lesion completeness but leave the criterion’s full-width sampling requirement unmet.
results.quote: In these mice, total axon regrowth past lesion centers was over 100-fold greater than SCI-only or SCI plus empty depots

results.finding: Adult rats after severe crush showed no detectable locomotor improvement with repair, with n=6 per locomotor group.
results.detail: The conduction response was evoked by spinal stimulation under anaesthesia. The locomotor experiment did not include rehabilitation.
results.quote: As in mice, over-ground locomotion of rats did not improve in these experiments that probed mechanisms required for axon regrowth but did not provide rehabilitation to elicit use-dependent plasticity

results.finding: In adult mice after complete T8 crush, traced corticospinal axons reached >7 mm beyond the lesion with combined treatment (n=10).
results.detail: The authors excluded three animals that failed their lesion-completeness checks.
results.quote:
This effect was slightly increased
further by the combination of PTEN −/− and AAV2-hIL-6, with
the longest axons reaching >7 mm (Fig. 2d, h, i and Fig. S4a).

results.finding: After complete crush, serotonergic depletion returned treated adult mice to injured-control locomotor scores within 1 day (n=6 per group).
results.detail: Corticospinal labeling remained intact after serotonergic depletion, and uninjured mice retained nearly normal open-field movement.
results.quote:
Thus, AAV2-hIL-6-mediated locomo-
tory recovery depended on RpST regeneration, even though
AAV2-hIL-6 had not been applied to the brain stem where the
serotonergic ﬁbers originated.

results.finding: Adult mice given acute AAV2-hIL-6 after complete crush reached a mean Basso Mouse Scale score of about 4 (n=9 treated, n=7 controls).
results.detail: The six-week intervention was serotonergic depletion to test the mechanism of recovery. Repair had already begun on the day of injury.
results.quote:
However, AAV2-hIL-6 treatment increased the BMS score to ∼4b y
restoring plantar stepping with full hindlimb weight support,
followed by lift-off, forward limb advancement, and reestablish-
ment of weight support at initial contact in most of the animals
(Fig. 3a, b and Fig. S6b; Supplementary video 3).

results.finding: In four grafted adult rhesus macaques after cervical hemisection, graft-derived axons reached up to 39 mm caudal to the lesion.
results.detail: The hemicontusion model also retained host tissue on the injured side.
results.quote: Graft-derived axons were present up to 39 mm caudal to the lesion.

results.finding: After cervical hemisection in eight adult rhesus macaques, graft recipients had 9.2-fold higher final skilled object retrieval success than controls.
results.detail: The graft comparison tested the treatment as a whole. Axon counts showed no significant correlation with recovery in either cohort.
results.quote: Overall, the performance of the grafted group exceeded that of the lesioned control group 9.2-fold on the final session of testing (mean fine object retrieval success of 53.4% ± 19.2% in grafted monkeys compared to 5.8% ± 5.4% in lesioned controls).

results.finding: In the first-in-human iPSC neural progenitor cell trial (n = 4), the first participant with cervical AIS A injury received a graft 25 days after injury.
results.quote: Here we report results from a first-in-human, open-label study of iPSC-NS/PC transplantation in four patients with subacute cervical complete SCI.

results.finding: After iPSC neural progenitor cell transplantation for subacute cervical AIS A injury, 2 of 4 participants showed some voluntary motor recovery below the lesion.
results.detail: Lower-extremity motor scores rose from 0 to 2 and from 8 to 39 in the two participants whose AIS grades improved. The registry comparison used total motor scores, which are broader than the below-lesion outcome.
results.quote: Improvement in AIS grade was noted in two participants, one from A to C and another from A to D, consistent with partial recovery of sensory function and voluntary motor activity below the injury level.

results.finding: Adult rats in the anatomy cohort (n=5/group) showed traced corticospinal axons crossing the lesion area 3 months after NT3-chitosan repair.
results.detail: The serial longitudinal sections described in the methods were used to quantify cell markers. The paper does not report a full-width histological check for spared fibres.
results.quote: CST axonal regeneration across the lesion area did occur in NT3-tube and NT3-gel groups, whereas no axonal extension into the lesion core was observed with the LC group

results.finding: After bridge resection, treated adult rats (n=8/group) fell to the lesion-control level on the 21-point BBB walking scale.
results.detail: The reported comparison uses lesion controls. The text does not describe a matched resection procedure in controls.
results.quote: After the regenerated tissue resection, the BBB scores for NT3-tube group and the NT3-gel group decreased to the level of the LC group.

results.finding: Adult rats (n=8/group) had better hindlimb walking than lesion controls after NT3-chitosan repair begun 3 months after complete transection.
results.quote: At 4 weeks after the second operation and thereafter, the NT3-tube group and the NT3-gel group showed significantly higher BBB scores compared with the LC group.

results.finding: Rats with complete spinal cord transection improved more in climbing after chronic glial grafting (n = 5 grafted, 6 injured controls, p = 0.002).
results.detail: The p-value comes from the chronic-stage Results text. The Figure 3 caption reports p = 0.001 for the chronic comparison.
results.quote: Before transplantation Chr rats behaved in the climbing test similar to Non-T rats, and after transplantation (4 months after injury) they recovered function more than Non-T rats (p = 0.002).

results.finding: A registered trial administered autologous sural nerve grafts to 12 patients with thoracic paraplegia at least 12 months after injury.
results.detail: Table 1 gives individual injury durations. The preceding animal studies evaluated spinal cord fusion and a different graft procedure.
results.quote: We conducted a clinical trial (ChiCTR2000030788) and performed SNT in 12 fully paraplegic patients due to SCI between T1 and T12.

title = "Voluntary motor recovery after chronic paralysis from complete spinal cord transection". Reason: The title omits the chronic paralysis that defines the human indication.

definition = "After at least 12 months of paralysis, a person regains intentional movement below a complete spinal cord transection because biological connections carry commands from the brain across the original gap. Complete transection means the cord was severed across its entire width. Grade A on the American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale records the absence of sensory and motor function in the lowest sacral segments. In a 2014 case, a man graded AIS A regained some voluntary leg movement after grafting and rehabilitation, but a 2-mm rim of tissue had connected the cord ends before surgery.". Reason: The definition leaves AIS unexplained and omits the human case that illustrates why the anatomical distinction matters.

goal.need = "In 2021, about 15.4 million people lived with spinal cord injury worldwide. The number with chronic anatomical transection is unknown. Rehabilitation and assistive equipment help people manage daily activities. When the cord is fully severed, no surviving nerve fibres cross the gap to carry commands from the brain. Depending on the injury level and the movement recovered, a person could eat, dress or walk with less help. Bowel and bladder control are separate goals.". Reason: The existing rationale explains a diagnostic distinction but omits what restored movement could let a person do.

add statement by Wrocław Walk Again programme, sponsored by the Nicholls Spinal Injury Foundation, 2019: "functional regeneration of severed spinal cord axons". Reason: The Wrocław programme explicitly names functional regeneration after anatomically complete transection as a human research goal.

edit completion: criterion = "A multicentre, controlled Phase 3 trial shows a statistically significant benefit on a prespecified measure of voluntary movement below the lesion, with an acceptable adverse-event profile. Before repair, participants had documented discontinuity across the whole cord and at least 12 months of paralysis. Anatomical and physiological evidence attributes recovered transmission to the repair. The protocol justifies the between-group difference it is powered to detect by its clinical importance and specifies the statistical test and follow-up. Sensory recovery, a change in AIS grade or an evoked response alone cannot establish voluntary movement."; threshold_quote = "the minimal effect that has clinical relevance in the management of patients."; threshold_ref = 6; basis = "The ICCP panel defines the general Phase 3 trial convention and the basis for choosing a target effect size. The Atlas applies it to voluntary movement transmitted across a biologically repaired transection. The 12-month boundary comes from the clinical guideline's definition of chronic SCI. No external body identified a universal motor-score increment, follow-up interval or completion test for this exact indication."; refs = [6, 5, 2, 7]. Reason: The existing test calls for a prespecified effect size without stating the panel's requirement to justify it by its importance to patients.

edit m1: criterion = "In an adult mammal, tracing shows that previously severed axons extend beyond the lesion into spinal cord tissue on the far side. Systematic histological sampling across the full width of the cord documents lesion completeness and distinguishes regrowth from fibres spared by the injury."; refs = [8, 9, 20]. Reason: The criterion mixes the anatomical test with one paper's date, findings and sample count.

edit m2: title = "Regenerated connections make a causal contribution to movement after complete spinal cord injury."; criterion = "After an anatomically complete lesion in an adult mammal, an experiment links recovery of a measured movement to regenerated connections across the lesion. Selective inactivation is one such test: silencing the neurons whose axons regenerated impairs the recovered movement, while the same manipulation in an appropriate control group leaves movement intact."; set_by = "National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, RFA-NS-04-004, on establishing mechanisms of functional recovery. Squair and colleagues supply the selective-inactivation test."; set_by_kind = "government_programme"; threshold_quote = "elucidate the mechanisms that underlie recovery induced by\n    neuroprotection or repair strategies in animal models"; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7, 10]. Reason: The current criterion conflates the causal test with results from two different lesion models and treats one experiment's silencing method as the required protocol.

add milestone after m2: "Biological repair begun after complete cord injury becomes chronic improves motor function in rodents.". Reason: The sequence jumps from repair around the time of injury to human treatment after prolonged paralysis, skipping the recommended chronic animal model.

edit m3: criterion = "After preclinical safety evaluation, a Phase 1 study administers the biological repair to its first participant with documented anatomical discontinuity across the whole spinal cord and paralysis lasting at least 12 months before treatment."; refs = [6, 5, 14]. Reason: The first-use criterion includes two reports outside the indication and leaves the required duration of paralysis implicit.

edit m4: criterion = "A controlled Phase 2 study finds a benefit of biological repair on a measure of voluntary movement below the lesion. Participants had documented discontinuity across the whole cord and at least 12 months of paralysis before treatment. The person measuring the outcome or evaluating the outcome data is blinded to treatment assignment."; refs = [6, 5, 14, 19]. Reason: The Phase 2 criterion includes registry history and a search result where readers need the comparison, outcome and blinding requirement.
remove not found 2. Reason: The registry-access note describes a website display issue, while reference 14 already supplies the study record.

add not found: "No academy or spinal cord society position was found that rejects pursuing voluntary motor recovery after chronic anatomical transection.". Reason: The available institutional statements do not resolve whether a body with standing disputes this precise goal.
remove statement 1. Reason: The NICHD statement identifies a topic in biochemistry without naming functional repair of a transected cord as its goal.
